questions.question: [Planetary Motion & Gravity] Q: State Kepler's three laws of planetary motion.
questions.correctAnswer: 1st: Planets orbit in ellipses with the Sun at one focus. 2nd: A line from planet to Sun sweeps equal areas in equal times. 3rd: T² is proportional to a³.
questions.explanation: 1st: Planets orbit in ellipses with the Sun at one focus. 2nd: A line from planet to Sun sweeps equal areas in equal times. 3rd: T² is proportional to a³.

questions.question: [Planetary Motion & Gravity] Q: Why do planets move faster at perihelion?
questions.correctAnswer: Because of Kepler's second law — equal areas are swept in equal times, so the planet must move faster when closer to the Sun to cover the same area.
questions.explanation: Because of Kepler's second law — equal areas are swept in equal times, so the planet must move faster when closer to the Sun to cover the same area.

questions.question: [Planetary Motion & Gravity] Q: State Newton's law of gravitation and explain each term.
questions.correctAnswer: F = GMm/r². F is the gravitational force, G is the gravitational constant, M and m are the two masses, and r is the distance between their centres.
questions.explanation: F = GMm/r². F is the gravitational force, G is the gravitational constant, M and m are the two masses, and r is the distance between their centres.

questions.question: [Star Properties & Classification] Q: What is the difference between apparent and absolute magnitude?
questions.correctAnswer: Apparent magnitude is how bright a star looks from Earth. Absolute magnitude is the brightness it would have if placed at a standard distance of 10 parsecs.
questions.explanation: Apparent magnitude is how bright a star looks from Earth. Absolute magnitude is the brightness it would have if placed at a standard distance of 10 parsecs.

questions.question: [Star Properties & Classification] Q: State the spectral classes from hottest to coolest.
questions.correctAnswer: O, B, A, F, G, K, M (mnemonic: Oh Be A Fine Girl/Guy, Kiss Me).
questions.explanation: O, B, A, F, G, K, M (mnemonic: Oh Be A Fine Girl/Guy, Kiss Me).

questions.question: [Star Properties & Classification] Q: How is stellar parallax used to measure distance?
questions.correctAnswer: A star's apparent shift against background stars is measured over 6 months. Distance in parsecs = 1/parallax angle in arcseconds.
questions.explanation: A star's apparent shift against background stars is measured over 6 months. Distance in parsecs = 1/parallax angle in arcseconds.

questions.question: [Stellar Lifecycle] Q: Describe the lifecycle of a star like the Sun.
questions.correctAnswer: Nebula → protostar → main sequence (hydrogen fusion) → red giant (helium fusion) → planetary nebula → white dwarf.
questions.explanation: Nebula → protostar → main sequence (hydrogen fusion) → red giant (helium fusion) → planetary nebula → white dwarf.

questions.question: [Stellar Lifecycle] Q: What happens to a star more than 8 times the mass of the Sun?
questions.correctAnswer: It becomes a red supergiant, undergoes further fusion stages up to iron, then explodes as a supernova. The core becomes a neutron star (if <3 M☉) or a black hole (if >3 M☉).
questions.explanation: It becomes a red supergiant, undergoes further fusion stages up to iron, then explodes as a supernova. The core becomes a neutron star (if <3 M☉) or a black hole (if >3 M☉).

questions.question: [Stellar Lifecycle] Q: What is the Chandrasekhar limit?
questions.correctAnswer: ~1.4 solar masses — the maximum mass a white dwarf can have. Above this, electron degeneracy pressure cannot support it and it collapses further.
questions.explanation: ~1.4 solar masses — the maximum mass a white dwarf can have. Above this, electron degeneracy pressure cannot support it and it collapses further.

questions.question: [The Hertzsprung-Russell Diagram] Q: What are the axes of the HR diagram?
questions.correctAnswer: Vertical axis: luminosity or absolute magnitude (increasing upward). Horizontal axis: temperature or spectral class (decreasing left to right — hot stars on the left).
questions.explanation: Vertical axis: luminosity or absolute magnitude (increasing upward). Horizontal axis: temperature or spectral class (decreasing left to right — hot stars on the left).

questions.question: [The Hertzsprung-Russell Diagram] Q: Where are white dwarfs found on the HR diagram and why?
questions.correctAnswer: Lower-left: they are hot (high temperature) but dim (low luminosity) because they are very small.
questions.explanation: Lower-left: they are hot (high temperature) but dim (low luminosity) because they are very small.

questions.question: [The Hertzsprung-Russell Diagram] Q: Why are red giants luminous despite being cool?
questions.correctAnswer: Because they have enormous surface area — luminosity depends on both temperature and radius (L ∝ R²T⁴), so a very large radius compensates for low temperature.
questions.explanation: Because they have enormous surface area — luminosity depends on both temperature and radius (L ∝ R²T⁴), so a very large radius compensates for low temperature.
